title: Internet Protocol

hero.subtitle: The foundational network layer protocol that routes packets across the global Internet

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol (IP) is the principal network-layer protocol of the Internet protocol suite. It provides the addressing and routing mechanism that enables packets to traverse multiple networks from source to destination.

IP is a connectionless, best-effort delivery service. It makes no guarantees about packet delivery, ordering, or integrity — those responsibilities are left to higher-layer protocols like TCP.

Every device on the Internet is identified by at least one IP address. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses, providing approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet Protocol (IP) provides addressing and routing so packets can cross multiple networks from source to destination. It is connectionless and best-effort: it does not guarantee delivery, order or integrity, which higher-layer protocols such as TCP handle. IPv4 uses 32-bit addresses.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
IP performs two fundamental functions:

Addressing
Each IP datagram carries a 32-bit source address and a 32-bit destination address. These addresses identify the sending and receiving hosts and enable routers to make forwarding decisions.
Fragmentation and Reassembly
When a datagram is too large for a network's Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU), IP can fragment it into smaller pieces. The destination host reassembles the fragments into the original datagram.

IP treats each datagram independently. Two successive datagrams from the same source to the same destination may take entirely different routes through the network.
sections.plainLanguage: IP does two things. It puts a 32-bit source and destination address on each datagram so routers can forward it. And when a datagram is too large for a network's maximum transmission unit (MTU), it splits it into fragments that the destination reassembles. Each datagram is handled independently.

sections.title: Specification
sections.content:
The IP specification defines the datagram format, addressing conventions, and the rules for fragmentation and reassembly.

Protocol Version4 (IPv4)
Address Size32 bits (4 octets)
Max Datagram Size65,535 bytes
Min Header Size20 bytes (no options)
Max Header Size60 bytes (with options)
Every host must accept576 bytes (and every module must forward 68)
sections.plainLanguage: This section sets the basic IPv4 limits. Addresses are 32 bits. A datagram can be up to 65,535 bytes, with a header of 20 to 60 bytes. Every host must accept datagrams of at least 576 bytes, and every module must forward at least 68.

sections.title: Addressing
sections.content:
IPv4 addresses are 32 bits long, typically written in dotted-decimal notation (e.g., 192.0.2.1). RFC 791 itself defines only classes a, b and c (plus an escape code for extended addressing); the D and E ranges below were assigned later. The classful ranges were:

A1.0.0.0 – 126.255.255.255 (16M hosts/net)
B128.0.0.0 – 191.255.255.255 (65K hosts/net)
C192.0.0.0 – 223.255.255.255 (254 hosts/net)
D224.0.0.0 – 239.255.255.255 (Multicast)
E240.0.0.0 – 255.255.255.255 (Reserved)

Classful addressing was wasteful and has been replaced by CIDR (Classless Inter-Domain Routing, RFC 4632) which allows arbitrary prefix lengths, enabling more efficient address allocation.
sections.plainLanguage: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four decimal numbers such as 192.0.2.1. RFC 791 defines address classes that split the address into a network part and a host part. Classful addressing was wasteful and was replaced by CIDR, which allows prefixes of any length.

sections.title: Fragmentation
sections.content:
When an IP datagram exceeds the MTU of the outgoing network, the router fragments the datagram into smaller pieces that fit:

Identification
A 16-bit field set by the sender. All fragments of the same datagram carry the same Identification value so the receiver can group them.
Fragment Offset
Indicates where in the original datagram this fragment belongs, measured in 8-byte units. This allows the receiver to reassemble fragments in the correct order.
More Fragments (MF) Flag
Set to 1 on all fragments except the last one. When a receiver gets a fragment with MF=0, it knows this is the final piece.
Don't Fragment (DF) Flag
When set, routers must not fragment this datagram. If it exceeds the MTU, the router discards it (and, per RFC 792, may report this with an ICMP "Fragmentation Needed" message).
sections.plainLanguage: When a datagram is larger than the next network's MTU, a router splits it into fragments. The Identification field groups fragments of one datagram, Fragment Offset gives each piece's position, and the More Fragments flag is set on all but the last. If Don't Fragment is set, the router discards the datagram instead.

sections.title: Header Format
sections.content: The header is at least 20 octets (five 32-bit words) and at most 60. The fields are fixed except Options and Padding, which are variable and not drawn below. In this RFC the second octet is the Type of Service: three precedence bits, then delay, throughput and reliability bits, then two reserved zero bits (modern networks reinterpret it as DSCP and ECN).
sections.plainLanguage: Every IP header is 20 to 60 bytes long. Its fixed fields cover the version, header length, type of service, total length, fragmentation information, time to live, protocol, checksum, and the source and destination addresses. Only the Options and Padding fields vary in length.

subtitle: The foundational network layer protocol that routes packets across the global Internet

plainLanguage.summary: IP puts source and destination addresses on each packet of data so that many networks can pass it along to the right host. It can fragment packets that are too large for a network. It does not guarantee that a packet arrives.

questions: what is in an ipv4 header
what is the time to live field

tldr.problem: Many different networks needed to be joined so that a host on one could send data to a host on another.
tldr.mechanism: Each datagram carries source and destination addresses in a header; gateways forward it hop by hop, fragmenting it when the next network's packets are smaller.
tldr.outcome: IP is connectionless and unreliable by design, so reliability is left to protocols like TCP. IPv4 is still the base of the Internet, with IPv6 growing beside it.

today: IPv4 is still carrying a huge share of Internet traffic, though IPv6 (RFC 8200) is now widely deployed alongside it. The class A/B/C scheme in this RFC was replaced by classless addressing (CIDR, RFC 4632), and the Type of Service byte was redefined as DSCP and ECN. The 32-bit address space ran out at the registries, which is why NAT is common.

items.label: Class a
items.desc: 7 bits of net, 24 bits of host

items.label: Class b
items.desc: 14 bits of net, 16 bits of host

items.label: Class c
items.desc: 21 bits of net, 8 bits of host

items.label: Extended
items.desc: Escape to extended addressing mode, undefined and reserved

fields.name: Version
fields.desc: The format of the internet header. Value 4 for this RFC.

fields.name: IHL
fields.desc: Internet Header Length in 32-bit words. Points to the beginning of the data. The minimum value is 5.

fields.name: Type of Service
fields.desc: Bits 0-2 precedence, bit 3 delay, bit 4 throughput, bit 5 reliability, bits 6-7 reserved (zero).

fields.name: Total Length
fields.desc: Length of the datagram in octets, including header and data. All hosts must accept datagrams up to 576 octets.

fields.name: Identification
fields.desc: Assigned by the sender to aid in assembling the fragments of a datagram.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Bit 0 reserved, must be zero. Bit 1 DF: 1 = Don't Fragment. Bit 2 MF: 1 = More Fragments.

fields.name: Fragment Offset
fields.desc: Where in the datagram this fragment belongs, in units of 8 octets. The first fragment has offset zero.

fields.name: Time to Live
fields.desc: Maximum time in seconds the datagram may remain in the internet system. Zero means it must be destroyed. Each module decrements it by at least one.

fields.name: Protocol
fields.desc: The next level protocol used in the data portion. Values are in Assigned Numbers (for example ICMP is 1, UDP is 17, TCP is 6).

fields.name: Header Checksum
fields.desc: Checksum on the header only, recomputed at each point the header changes. Computed with the field as zero.
